title: Right Patient, Right Tube: Identification and Wrong Blood in Tube
summary: Follow a tube from order to label, watch two tubes get swapped into a wrong-blood-in-tube error, and see how one hospital cut identification errors by 97%.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 3 Hits 2–3 (ordering errors, misidentification) and the WBIT idea from the Number Vault. The reviewer’s figures (“~1 in 1,000 specimens misidentified”, “~1 in 12,000 patients get blood intended for someone else”, WBIT 1.1 vs 2.7 per 1,000) were not found in the sources read; the lesson uses published figures instead and keeps the reviewer’s as pending.

objectives: Describe safe identification: two identifiers, matched to the request, with labeling at the bedside at collection.
Explain what a wrong-blood-in-tube error is and why the laboratory rarely detects it.
Interpret published identification-error rates and the interventions that reduce them.

scenes.title: Two patients, one name
scenes.altText: Two hospital beds side by side, both with wristbands reading “M. Santos”. A phlebotomist draws blood from the first bed, carries the unlabeled tubes to the nurses’ station and labels them there. A question mark hangs over the tube: whose blood is it really?

cues.text: Two patients in neighbouring beds share a name: M. Santos.
Blood is drawn from one bed, but the tubes are labeled later, out at the nurses’ station.
The label looks perfect. But whose blood is inside? The lab has no way to see it.

scenes.title: The safe path: right test, right patient, right label
scenes.altText: A path of four stations lights up in turn: “Right test ordered” → “Two identifiers checked (e.g., name and date of birth or ID number), matched to the request” → “Label at the bedside, at the time of collection” → “Barcode scan links tube to patient”. A tube travels along the path and gains a green check at each station.

cues.text: A good result starts before the needle. The first step is ordering the right test — a wrong or unneeded test is an error before any blood is drawn.
Next, identify the patient with at least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth or a hospital ID number, and match them to the request.
Then label the tubes at the bedside, at the time of collection, in front of the patient. Never label tubes ahead of time or later somewhere else.
Many hospitals add barcode scanning of the wristband and the tube label, so a computer confirms the match.
Each step closes a gap where the wrong blood could slip into the right-looking tube.

scenes.title: Wrong blood in tube
scenes.altText: The bedside step is skipped: two unlabeled tubes from beds 4A and 4B sit together on a tray, and their labels are swapped. The result for 4A now shows 4B’s values. A banner reads “WBIT: wrong blood in tube — the label is right, the blood is not.” A transfusion panel follows: New York data — about 1 in 19,000 red cell units given in error; most events outside the blood bank; phlebotomy errors 13% of events.

cues.text: Now skip the bedside step. Tubes from two patients wait unlabeled on the same tray.
At the station the labels go on — swapped. Each tube now carries a perfect label and the wrong person’s blood.
This is “wrong blood in tube,” or WBIT. Every result from that tube belongs to someone else, and the label gives no hint.
In blood banking this can kill. New York State data found about 1 in 19,000 red cell units given in error, with most events happening outside the blood bank.
Phlebotomy errors caused 13 percent of those events. That is why blood bank samples get the strictest identification of all.

scenes.title: In the lab: catching and preventing ID errors
scenes.altText: A hospital chart of specimen identification errors: 0.0511% of 2,000,345 specimens in 2005 (about 1 in 2,000) falling to 0.0015% in 2014 after a restrictive acceptance policy, barcode positive identification and automated labeling — a 97% reduction. A breakdown shows the emergency department had the highest baseline rate (0.106%). A calculator token shows 1,023 ÷ 2,000,345 ≈ 0.05%.

cues.text: How common are ID errors? One large hospital counted every specimen identification error for ten years.
In 2005, 1,023 of about 2 million specimens had ID errors: 0.05 percent, or roughly 1 in 2,000. The emergency department had the highest rate.
They rejected unlabeled or mislabeled specimens, added barcode identification and automated labeling. By 2014 the rate fell to 0.0015 percent — a 97 percent drop.
Wrong-blood-in-tube errors are the hardest to catch: the lab only notices when a result clashes with the patient’s history, such as a failed delta check or a different blood group.
So the lab’s best tool is prevention at the bedside — and refusing specimens whose identity is in doubt.

props.label: One hospital · 10 years · every ID error counted
WBIT clue: result clashes with history (delta check)
Best defense: prevention at the bedside

scenes.title: ID traps
scenes.altText: Three cards: “Room number is an identifier” → crossed out, “Use two identifiers (name + date of birth or ID number)”; “Label tubes before drawing to save time” → crossed out, “Label at the bedside, at collection”; “Relabel a mislabeled tube” → crossed out, “Reject and recollect when identity is in doubt”.

cues.text: Trap: using a bed or room number to identify the patient. Patients move; use two personal identifiers, such as name and date of birth or an ID number.
Trap: labeling tubes before the draw to save time. Pre-labeled tubes are easily used on the wrong patient. Label at the bedside, at collection.
Trap: fixing a mislabeled tube by relabeling it. If identity is in doubt, the safe policy is to reject the specimen and recollect.

scenes.title: Ask · Match · Label — in the room
scenes.altText: Memory aid: three stamps in a row — ASK (the patient states name and date of birth), MATCH (to the wristband and request), LABEL (at the bedside) — under a banner “in the room”. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: Ask, Match, Label — in the room. Ask the patient to state their name and date of birth, match it to the wristband and request, and label before you leave.
If any step fails, stop: no label, no test.
Where it breaks: unconscious or confused patients cannot answer, so you rely on the wristband and local policy; and blood bank samples often need extra steps such as special bands or a second sample.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: A tube with a green check passes three tokens: “Right test”, “Two identifiers”, “Labeled at the bedside”.

cues.text: Most lab errors happen before the analyzer, so order the right test, identify every patient with two identifiers, and label tubes at the bedside at the time of collection — because a wrong-blood-in-tube error looks perfect to the lab.

explanation.what: Plain language: before any test, make sure it is the right test, the right person and the right label — because a tube with a perfect label and someone else’s blood fools everyone. Scientific terms: preanalytical identification errors include test-request errors, patient misidentification and mislabeling; wrong blood in tube (WBIT) is a specimen labeled for one patient but containing another patient’s blood.
explanation.why: Most laboratory errors occur outside the analytical phase. Labeling away from the patient lets tubes be swapped; pre-labeled tubes can be used on the wrong person. The analyzer measures whatever blood is in the tube, so WBIT results look valid unless they clash with the patient’s history.
explanation.measure: Labs track identification-error rates (one hospital: 0.0511% in 2005 → 0.0015% in 2014 after interventions) and use delta checks and blood-group history to catch some WBIT. In New York State, about 1 in 19,000 red cell units was given in error, with phlebotomy errors in 13% of events.
explanation.differs: Mislabel (label wrong or missing — often visible) vs WBIT (label correct for the request but blood from someone else — invisible). Identifier (name, date of birth, ID number) vs location (room or bed number).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: how many identifiers (at least two), when to label (at the bedside, at collection), what to do with a mislabeled specimen (reject and recollect), why WBIT is dangerous, and which phase has the most errors (preanalytical).

mnemonic.text: Ask · Match · Label — in the room.
mnemonic.explanation: Ask the patient to state name and date of birth, match to the wristband and request, and label in the room before leaving.
mnemonic.limitation: Unconscious, confused or very young patients cannot state their details, so staff rely on the wristband and local policy. Blood bank samples may need extra safeguards such as special bands or a second confirming sample. The aid does not cover choosing the right test.

analogyLimitations: The two-patients-one-name scenario is invented to show the risk.
Error rates come from one hospital and one state; other settings differ.
The barcode step is simplified; systems vary.
The 2005 and 2014 bars are not drawn to scale (the true ratio is about 34 : 1).
takeaway: Most lab errors happen before the analyzer, so order the right test, identify every patient with two identifiers, and label tubes at the bedside at the time of collection — because a wrong-blood-in-tube error looks perfect to the lab.

questions.stem: Which practice best prevents patient misidentification during blood collection?

options.text: Confirm two identifiers against the request and label the tubes at the bedside at the time of collection
options.rationale: Correct. At least two identifiers plus labeling at collection, in front of the patient, closes the main gaps.

options.text: Pre-label tubes at the nurses’ station before entering the room
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pre-labeled tubes are easily used on the wrong patient.

options.text: Identify the patient by room and bed number
options.rationale: Incorrect. Locations are not identifiers; patients move and share rooms.

options.text: Label tubes back in the lab where printers are available
options.rationale: Incorrect. Labeling away from the patient allows swaps — the main cause of WBIT.

questions.stem: A patient’s new blood type result differs from the type on record, although the tube label is correct and complete. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Wrong blood in tube — the correctly labeled tube contains another patient’s blood
options.rationale: Correct. WBIT is detected only when results clash with history; a historical blood-group mismatch is a classic clue.

options.text: An analytical error, since the label is correct
options.rationale: Incorrect. A correct label does not prove the blood belongs to the patient; identification errors are far more common than analytical errors.

options.text: The patient’s blood type changed naturally
options.rationale: Incorrect. ABO type does not change in ordinary circumstances; a mismatch points to a specimen problem.
Incorrect. Hemolysis affects many tests but does not change a patient’s ABO group.

questions.stem: A hospital found 1,023 identification errors among 2,000,345 specimens. About what rate is this?

options.rationale: Incorrect. This is 100 times too high — a decimal slip.
Incorrect. This is 10 times too high.
Incorrect. This is 10 times too low.

claims.text: Use at least two patient identifiers and attach labels at the time of collection.
One hospital’s ID-error rate fell from 0.0511% (2005) to 0.0015% (2014) after restrictive acceptance, barcode ID and automated labeling; the ED had the highest baseline rate.
WBIT errors are usually undetectable unless results clash with expectations or history.
In New York State, about 1 in 19,000 RBC units was given in error; about half of events occurred outside the blood bank; phlebotomy errors caused 13%.
Most laboratory errors occur outside the analytical phase.
Wrong test or panel selection at ordering is the most frequent preanalytical error (attributed to Bonini 2002).
claims.note: Not stated in the Bonini 2002 abstract; full text not read.

claims.text: About 1 in 1,000 specimens is misidentified at collection; about 1 in 12,000 patients receives blood intended for someone else; WBIT 1.1 per 1,000 for trained phlebotomists vs 2.7 per 1,000 for other staff.
claims.note: Not found in sources read (register flag rv-id-rates).

claims.text: Room and bed numbers are not acceptable identifiers; mislabeled specimens should be rejected and recollected.
claims.note: Common policy, consistent with Ning 2016’s restrictive acceptance policy, but not stated in the passages read.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer’s identification and transfusion-error rates could not be matched to a source read; Linden 2000 reports 1 in 19,000 RBC units, not 1 in 12,000 patients (register flag rv-id-rates).
